title: Australian Billionaire Politician Clive Palmer and His Wanted Nephew Had Vanuatu Diplomatic Passports
content:
Australian billionaire politician Clive Palmer, along with his wife and nephew, received diplomatic passports and appointments from Vanuatu, according to a parliamentary report in the Pacific nation.

Vanuatu’s Public Accounts Committee recently released a report into the issuance of diplomatic passports by officials. Among more than two dozen cancelled diplomatic passports listed in an appendix to the report, OCCRP found Palmer and his two family members.

Palmer was appointed as a Vanuatu trade commissioner on May 29, 2023. Two months earlier, on March 17, Vanuatu gave a similar posting to his nephew, Clive Mensink — who was wanted by Australian authorities at the time for contempt of court in a case about a corporate collapse.

Palmer’s wife, Anna, was made a Vanuatu trade commissioner at the same time as her husband.

All three had their diplomatic passports cancelled in September of 2025, the appendix shows, as Vanuatu cracked down on the issuance of such documents to foreign and dual citizens.

“Mr. Palmer was invited to be an ambassador to the previous Vanuatu Government because of his experience in international trade,” said Andrew Crook, a spokesman for the billionaire.

title: UK Hacker Sentenced to Seven Years, Then Released
content:
British hacker Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced to seven years in prison on Monday for a series of cyberattacks targeting major international companies, but was released from custody the same day after the court took into account time he had already spent in detention.

Woolwich Crown Court initially imposed a nine-year sentence, reducing it by two years to reflect time Kurtaj had spent under a hospital order. He was subsequently released on license, meaning he remains subject to supervision and conditions.

Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group, pleaded guilty on November 16 to six offenses, including fraud, four violations of the Computer Misuse Act and illegally possessing a mobile phone in prison. Seven additional charges were left on file.

His attacks between 2020 and 2022 targeted companies including Uber, Revolut, telecommunications operators BT and EE, and Rockstar Games, the developer of the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

title: European Parts Made in 2026 Found in Russian Drones
content:
European electronic components manufactured as recently as February 2026 have been found in Russian drones used against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, highlighting Russia's continued access to foreign technology despite years of Western sanctions.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said investigators have identified more than 16,000 foreign-made components in Russian drones, missiles and other weapons — the highest figure reported by Ukrainian authorities to date.

“Based on inspections of incident sites, expert examinations and analysis of physical evidence, more than 16,000 foreign-made components have been identified so far,” the office told OCCRP and its partners, the Kyiv Independent, De Tijd and Paper Trail Media. 

“These components are used in drones, missiles and other weapons in service with the aggressor state [Russia] (…) and bear the markings of companies from over 30 countries,” it said.

Ukraine's military intelligence has published details of more than 6,300 foreign-made components found in Russian weapons on its War & Sanctions website.

title: Citing Trafficking Risks, Georgia Plans Total Ban on Surrogacy
content:
Georgia’s ruling party has announced plans to impose a complete ban on surrogacy, framing the move as a campaign against human trafficking and the exploitation of women, even as opposition leaders and fertility doctors accused the government of bowing to the Orthodox Church and threatening families struggling with infertility.

Irakli Kirtskhalia, a lawmaker with the governing Georgian Dream party, said after a meeting of the parliamentary majority that legislation was being drafted to outlaw the practice entirely, though in vitro fertilization would remain legal. Georgia’s surrogacy market has expanded significantly since 2023, Kirtskhalia said, adding that the party had consulted both executive authorities and the Georgian Patriarchate.

“We understand well that banning surrogacy may have a certain economic impact; however, we believe that economic benefits cannot outweigh these risks and ethical issues,” he said.

title: Iraq’s Oil Minister Denies Ouster Rumors as Najaf Smuggling Scandal Widens
content:
Iraq’s Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair al-Abadi on Monday denied media reports  that prime minister Ali Al Zaidi was considering dismissing him following the discovery of possible oil smuggling operations in the Iraqi province of Najaf this weekend. 

"The issue of resignation is completely unfounded," al-Abadi said in a statement, adding that he fully supports the government’s anti-corruption efforts.

Al-Abadi’s reaction came after Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council on Saturday said a court issued arrest warrants against the head of the Energy Committee at the Najaf Provincial Council and his brother after an investigating judge conducted a field inspection in a plot of land belonging to the siblings.

The judge found “encroachment on one of the oil pipelines in the Najaf Governorate,” the statement said, adding that the two men “had previously dug a trench surrounding the plot of land on all sides, hindering access and preventing people from observing the activities taking place there.”

title: U.K. Seizes $72 Million Tied to Singapore Scandal, Drawing Scrutiny Over Early Deals
content:
Britain’s National Crime Agency has seized more than $70 million in properties tied to Singapore’s $2.3 billion money-laundering scandal, an outcome which, although hailed as a success in combating financial crime, has been criticized by an expert as a “missed opportunity” for the larger recoveries and greater accountability that a trial would likely have brought.

The NCA named last week Su Haijin and Xu Haika as two individuals “linked to an international money laundering network that had agreed to hand over around £55 million ($72.1 million) in assets after being pursued by the NCA”, in a settlement that was approved by the U.K. High Court.

OCCRP has reported extensively on the U.K. and global asset portfolio of both men, including Su Haijin’s purchase of a townhouse on Oxford Street, and Xu Haika’s purchases of multiple luxury apartments further down the same bustling high street. 

“These settlements are in the public interest, avoiding protracted and costly High Court litigation while enabling our resources to be redirected towards new investigations," said Gareth Jones, Branch Commander for Asset Denial at the National Crime Agency.

title: US Sanctions Italian Mafia Group in Canada and Australian Biker Gang with Global Footprint
content:
The latest U.S. sanctions against organized crime stretch from Canada, home to a powerful faction of an Italian mafia group, to Australia where an outlaw motorcycle gang grew into an international drug dealing organization.

Both the Comancheros motorcycle gang and the Toronto-based ‘Ndrangheta mafia faction have ties to Mexican cocaine cartels, according to a statement on Thursday by the U.S. Treasury Department. 

“The Comancheros and the ‘Ndrangheta operate sophisticated transnational criminal networks that facilitate large-scale drug trafficking and money laundering,” the Treasury said.

Three of the sanctioned alleged ‘Ndrangheta members were featured in a multi-part investigation into the Canadian faction published in 2024 by OCCRP, the Toronto Star, and La Repubblica.

One article revealed that Angelo Figliomeni, the group’s alleged boss, was in contact with Toronto-area real estate developers, and was linked to a sprawling property empire.

title: Wine Distributor Targeted in Latest US Prince Group Sanctions Owns Warehouse Unit in London
content:
A man sanctioned this month for his alleged role in the Prince Group — a Cambodian conglomerate accused by the U.S. of operating major cyber-scams — controls a warehouse unit in London through his now-sanctioned wine distribution company, property documents show.

The U.S. Treasury Department imposed its third round of sanctions on the Prince Group on November 5, designating it as a “Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO)” and alleging it was involved in “cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking.”

A Prince Group spokesperson told OCCRP the Treasury Department has “no support for any of their latest allegations,” adding: “Once again, the U.S. Government has issued new sanctions with zero factual basis for their claims.”

Included among the newly-sanctioned entities and individuals was Chinese-born Qiu Yong, 39, who holds citizenships from Cambodia, Saint Lucia and Turkey, according to the Treasury Department.

title: Accused South American Drug Lord Faces US Trial after Judge Rejects Motions
content:
Sebastián Marset, an accused South American drug lord, appears headed for a January jury trial after a federal judge in Virginia this week rejected multiple efforts by the defense to dismiss charges.

U.S. District Judge Rossie Alston Jr. on Tuesday rejected arguments from Marset’s lawyers that the Uruguayan national was being subjected to a vindictive prosecution and misconduct by prosecutors.

Marset’s defense team had argued their client’s Miranda rights, which protect against self-incrimination, were violated when agents from the Drug Enforcement Administration interviewed him without a lawyer present.

But the judge held that Marset had initiated some of the conversations after his arrest in southern Bolivia and was not coerced into talking with DEA agents during his expulsion to Peru and subsequent transfer to the United States and custody in Virginia.

The judge also rejected the defense’s “fruit of the poisonous tree” motion that asserted that evidence should be excluded because it was obtained improperly.

title: The EU Could be Tracking Irish Alumina Shipments to Russia Amid Defense-Industry Scrutiny
content:
The European Commission has proposed new reporting rules on alumina exports to Russia amid concerns that output from a Russian-owned refinery in Ireland is feeding Russia’s weapons industry, requiring the Aughinish Alumina plant in County Limerick to disclose its Russian shipments and customers to Dublin and European Union partners.

“We can confirm that in the 22nd sanctions package we have proposed to include a reporting mechanism for all aluminium oxide trade with Russia,” European Commission spokesperson Siobhan McGarry told OCCRP. “This would include the Aughinish plant while not limited to it.”

The measure will allow the union “to establish a complete picture of alumina flows between the EU and Russia to confirm that it does not end up directly or indirectly being used in Russia’s military equipment,” McGarry added.

The proposal follows a March investigation by OCCRP and its partners — iStories, KibOrg, De Tijd, The Irish Times, The Guardian, and Delfi — that exposed links between the Irish refinery and Russian defense contractors.
